selected.hook_line: If water can crush an air pocket, why not your whole body?
selected.viewer_expectation: Deeper water should squeeze every part of a human body in the same way.
selected.visible_contradiction: Inside one pressure chamber, an air-filled bulb shrinks while a water-filled bulb beside it barely changes.
selected.frame_zero: Two clear flexible bulbs sit under pressure: the air-filled one is visibly smaller, while the water-filled one keeps its shape.
selected.character_action: The captain compares the two bulbs, watches the difference grow, then aims his spyglass toward the chamber.
selected.reaction: A raised eyebrow and a short thoughtful pause.
selected.activity: comparing how trapped air and water respond to the same pressure
selected.topic_link: Most body tissue contains much more water than gas, so trapped air changes far more under rising pressure.
selected.factual_anchor: Water and body tissues compress very little compared with air. Underwater pressure rises with depth, so air-filled spaces remain a major problem even if breathing is possible.
selected.payoff: Breathing removes one limit, not pressure. Air spaces must equalize, and very high pressure can also disturb normal nerve and body function.

entry_bridge.a_end: The captain faces the chamber with the spyglass raised toward the two bulbs.
entry_bridge.b_start: From behind his visible eye, the small eyepiece is near his face and the larger objective points toward the chamber.
entry_bridge.reveal: The view moves from the shrinking air bulb to the same pressure acting on a human body.
entry_bridge.world_entry: Underwater body cutaway: tissue keeps nearly the same volume while a small trapped air pocket is squeezed.

novelty.reveal_family: pressure affects gas far more than water-rich tissue
